Dysfunctional SAPS Stock-Outs

By: Eugene Botha | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
....SAPS seems to be imploding and can't do proper policing

Unique Selling Point:
Matter of National concern

Summary:
It seems that even good police officers cannot do their jobs properly because where procurement is supposed to happen, things have grinded to a halt. Most software is not licensed.No new tenders are awarded for crucial consumables, and crucial systems have been ordered to shut down for non-payment. All of it compromises the Criminal Justice system in its entirety

Further information:
We have been trying to get Keith Keating to speak about the Police Firearm Tracking system, the police's biometric system and the evidence control system. The police is using it illegally, despite court orders en a letter from the Police Comissioner.

In addition there are problems in the following areas:

1. DIGITAL FORENSICS

The South African Police Service’s (SAPS) cybercrime unit has been forced to drop investigations into hundreds of cases because software licenses have not been paid. A report in the Sunday Times revealed that investigations into organised crimes, hacking and EFT scams have been halted due to expired software licenses for equipment used to decode and interpret cellphone data. Sunday Times 2018.

Organized crime, terrorism, cash in transit heists, paedophiles, child porn, crypto scams,etc.

• XRY – Cell phone
• Cellebrite Touch -- Cell phone
• FDK – Computer
• Encase – Computer
• X-ways – Computer
• Passware – password recovery, de-cription
• Amptus – CCTV FOOTAGE
• IEF – On-line artefact extraction
• Host of other software not up to date

SAPS sections using it at least 5
• Crime Intelligence 22
• TISC -- Technological Investigation Support Centre - speurders
• Hawks & DFL – commercial crimes
• Warrooms in Provinces
• Forensic Lab

Contracts expire 2018, Peter skryf brief, geen reply
License expired? Letter by Head of Legal Div Commissioner Legal Sally Khan 20 March 2018
No hardware, software, no training
193 000 members, 25 000 detectives, 3800 field workers
About 50 staff to service whole police force
About 26 XRY licences country wide

Regions: no services --have to travel long distances

Backlog -- Natal – 150 computers, 400 phones

Cases thrown out

No money spent on Digital Forensics --- Compare to R1,2 Billion on VIP protection



2. FORENSICS LAB
• No new contracts, no consumables
• Examples: Little girl IDTake 2 months, Karabo – 8 hours ID
• 3x tenders cancelled, No tender out, Buy on quote – not more than 3 times (3 quotes) treasury has informed them that they must stop – Less than R500 000. No opne tender process, illegal in terms of procurement practices.
• Powder – not even lift fingerprints – embarrassment
• No crime scene collecting kits
• How are systems working – nobody knows how the systems, no back-up
• DNA lab – bought no supplies, chemicals, etc. Big machine not working.
• Rapid DNA profile kit – just not buying, Pretoria Cape Town, 3 machines for kits, couple of million. Karabo Mokoena – 8 hours, little girl identified – 2.5 months.
• Used to be 1 General and 2 Brigadiers. Now 6 gererals and 12 Brigadiers
• Experts daag by hof op sonder papier – Xerox het all hulle masjiene teruggevat – non-payment, no contract in place.
• Back-up of all data – can be restored, how long will it take? Nobody knows


3. LIGHT SOURCES

• 1800 kits bought
• Normal crime scene: 2 prints, with lights 20
• No contract, no service, no calibration, no parts.
• Technology not used.


4. POLICE APP

• Police app: Police stations and anonymous tips
• Could not run the previous system
• Vodacom app – not anonymous


5. IBIS INTEGRATED BALLISTICS IDENTIFICATION SYSTEM
Col Burger Kloppers kloppersb@saps.gov.za 012 845 5781
Sole supplier, no agents
Wants 6 suppliers to tender – no contract – month to month


6. NO TRAINING FOR THE LAST 18 MONTHS
Cyber, crime scene, new lab tech, light sources
Western Cape Warroom


7. WINDOWS 7
Police runs on Windows 7
All systems need to be re-written to be compatible with Windows 10
Windows 7 support stops 14/1/2019


8. NO BULLETS
• Consequences for training, firearm-proficiency tests, permits
• Ongoing for 2 years


9. MAIN SOURCES

• Danny Myburgh

Script:


V/O:
On the 3rd of April 2018 the body of Virgil Domingo was discovered next to a road in the south of Johannesburg. Her brother Rodney Krotz says her family had been looking for her for days, when he came across a news report online.
Rodney Krotz:
And how they described the body they found in the South of Johannesburg; I instantly knew it was my sister.
V/O:
The two of them had been very close.
Rodney Krotz:
We shared the same birthday, we worked together. She was like that one person whenever something was not going right in my life, I knew I could count on her.
V/O:
Virgil’s death was a mystery, but there was a lot of evidence left behind.
Rodney Krotz:
There was some things that were very suspicious at the house, like blood stains against the wall, against the headboard.
V/O:
Virgil also had a blue eye and a bite mark.
Rodney Krotz:
Forensic teams came out to check if there were any possible leads. When they came that evening on a Tuesday, they were in her room for 3 hours.
V/O:
Krotz was confident that with plenty of evidence such as fingerprints, blood samples and DNA left behind, police would be able to process the crime scene and solve the case. His hopes were dashed. He says there’s been no feedback for nearly two years. At the time the police’s undertaking around toxi-co-logical testing came as a big surprise.
Rodney Krotz:
According to the investigating officer the toxicology and histology reports are going to take 5 years.
V/O:
Such an incomplete investigation creates many loose ends.
Rodney Krotz:
Well she had a life cover, which we can’t claim because they need to know what the cause of death was.
V/O:
Police investigations such as this one, that yield no results are worrying.

Even more worrying is the fact that Krotz sister’s case is not isolated – there are countless others. And contributing to this are backlogs in processing evidence, for example there is currently a backlog of 23 000 DNA samples.

Gareth Newham of the Institute for Security Studies says the Police’s investigative capabilities have been deteriorating steadily.
Gareth Newham:
The evidence that there has been a deterioration in the South African Police Service since 2012 is in the annual reports. You see big reductions in the detection rate for example in 2012 the detection rate for murder was almost 32%. Which means that they were able to solve 32% of the cases reported. It has dropped to 20% in the most recent report and you see that for other crimes.
V/O:
South Africa’s crime investigation and forensic services are suffering in a number of problem areas.

CRIME SCENE INVESTIGATION

V/O:
Crime scene investigators have reported that conditions in the South African Police Service have deteriorated to such an extent that they cannot investigate crime properly. Nationwide CSI officers have basically run out of fingerprint brushes and powders.
SOURCE 1:
But at the end of the day, we don’t have any powders, we don’t have any brushes, we don’t have any lifters. Due to the procurement process.
LINK:
This is a complete fingerprint kit. It has all the brushes, the powders, the lifting tape. But these are in short supply in SA because no tender has been awarded to several years.
V/O:
Brigadier Vish Naidoo is the Police spokesperson. He says it’s a dispute with a supplier that’s resulted in the police service procuring consumables not through tenders, but on an ad hoc basis, through requests for quotations.
Vish Naidoo:
There has been, not a shortage, but a reduction of consumables, because we can only buy the consumables as and when they are needed.
V/O:
But the allegations go further.
LINK:
We were told that special light sources to detect bodily fluids and fingerprints have not been maintained and most are not serviceable because the supplier has not been paid.
V/O:
Brig Naidoo says when there were allegations of corruption against the supplier, the police terminated the contract.

All of this affects the processing of fingerprints nationwide.
Gareth Newham:
The total number of fingerprints that the police can sue to positively identify suspects in the last three years has declined by 45%. This means that there is almost 15 000 fewer positive hits on fingerprints in cases than there was 3 years ago in 2016/2017. More disturbingly the other forensic exhibits related to DNA, drug testing we’ve seen a massive decline the last three years. 202 000 fewer exhibits were analysed in the most recent financial year, than what was the case three years ago. These are not impressions; these are hard data the police provide and present itself to parliament on its performance.

FORENSIC SCIENCE LABS

V/O:
Allegations have also surfaced around a lack of consumables and lack of maintenance at forensic laboratories that are exacerbating backlogs.

Ferdinand Truter, a criminal defence lawyer, has seen backlogs cause delays in court and hamper convictions.
Masa:
In your experience, would you say there is a backlog in DNA tests blood tests, toxicology?

Ferdinand Truter:
Definitely, of a normal arrest for intoxication if you get a first appearance today and toxicology reports have been requested, the matter will be postponed between 6 and 12 months.
Q:
In the forensic Crime lab in Pretoria is the automated DNA system fully functional?

Vish Naidoo:
The automated, yes the automated DNA system, it’s got various stations. Alright. And I must tell you for each one there are consumables required. So we have to make sure that the consumables are there, which they are. As I said we buy them on procurement, on a quotation basis and the stations are working, the DNA stations. The backlog is not a growing backlog. So as we are moving forward the backlog is getting lesser and lesser.
V/O:
However, a leaked Information Note signed by three high ranking officials on 13 November, states that the machine is not functional through a lack of specialised consumables, and the absence of a contract for the repair and maintenance of instrumentation.

We posed that to Brig Naidoo by e-mail after his interview, but he said he wouldn’t respond to us any further.

DIGITAL FORENSICS LICENSES

V/O:
The field of Digital Forensics has suffered problems for years. Licences for critical software have not been renewed. It was reported in the media last year, but virtually nothing has been done – which seriously hampers digital forensic investigations.
SOURCE 2:
If you do not have a current license, you do not get updates. You need updates. to access the newer devices and computers with the latest security features. If you are not updated, you cannot extract data from new model cell phones, hard drives or computers.
Masa:
Can I just ask. In terms of your renewed licences. I want to go through a list of the following products and you tell me if you’ve got renewed licences here. XRY?
Vish Naidoo:
Um, just hold on there. That information was not requested from me, which I thinks is a bit disingenuous on your part, and therefor I would not be able to tell you which have and which does not have.
V/O:
But ours was not a disingenuous question – we had requested information around specific licences from Brig Naidoo by e-mail on September 6 and in several other e-mails and text messages.

BULLETS

V/O:
Reports surfaced over the last two years that the police have nearly run out of bullets as their supplier, DENEL, had stopped manufacturing. A shortage means that officers could not qualify to obtain permits to carry weapons, and many had to work without firearms.
Vish Naidoo:
The problem has since been resolved. We have entered into a 3 year contract with them. We already started to take delivery of ammunition in quite significant amounts.

FDA

V/O:
In 2017 the Police stopped payments to Forensic Data Analysts, the supplier of two important IT systems called the Firearm Permit System or FPS and the Property Control and Exhibit Management system or PCEM.

They said it was because of fraud, but no evidence has been produced to substantiate the claim.
LINK:
The FPS and PCEM systems are absolutely crucial for the functioning of the police and have relevance for the entire criminal justice system.
SOURCE 2
FPS is a biometric system that logs in police members, and keeps track of all firearms issued to the police. PCEM keeps electronic track of millions of exhibits and evidence. It secures and track the chain of custody of evidence.
V/O:
After months of non-payment FDA switched off the systems in April 2018. But the Police and the State Information Agency brought the systems back online.

Court cases up to the constitutional court level ordered the Police in scathing terms to either stop using the systems, or pay FDA to acquire the systems. This has not happened.
Source 2:
It is still being used – illegally.
V/O:
The two parties are currently in court-ordered talks. FDA declined to comment
Q:
The court rules that you do owe them money as SAPS.

Vish Naidoo:
Yes, but we are in discussion with them. We are in discussions with them and I said to you, I am not going to discuss with you or expose what discussions were are in. They know exactly what we are agreeing on.
V/O:
Shortages of basic crime investigation consumables seem to have been caused by the police avoiding the tender process and procuring goods and services through a quotation-based system. In addition, the Police returned R1,1 billion not spent, to Treasury last year.

Can this situation be improved or turned around? One way is to appropriate new technologies to address backlogs and help in the fight against crime.
V/O:
Jerenique Bayard of Intsika IT says there is amazing new technology available that can rapidly process DNA, yielding results in 90 minutes instead of weeks or months.
Jerenique Bayard:
When you arrest a person and you can hold him for 48 hours, the DNA act allows you to take a sample from him. But if you then get a result back 6 months later to say that guy is linked to other crimes, to find that guy again is the most difficult task.
V/O:
Having the results in less than 2 hours, is a real game changer.
Jerenique Bayard:
The sooner you know this is a person of interest and you can link that person to other cases, the quicker the case will be resolved.
V/O:
Policing can also benefit from a revision of the top structure of a police service that has grown out of proportion. The National Development Plan addresses this as a priority.
Gareth Newham:
As far back as 2012 the NDP identifies the serial crisis of the top management in the South African Police Service. For too long people have been appointed in key posts, top posts, without being properly vetted, without being properly assessed. And so now you’ve got this top structure which is quite large, you are talking about 200 generals. And we do not know how many of them should or should not be there. And that is why this issue now with the procurement is one of a whole range of areas where the police have deteriorated.
V/O
The NDP recommends a Police Board to reassess all those in top positions to make sure the right people are appointed in the right positions. That could turn the police around.
Gareth Newham:
It is possible to improve the police. There are really good people in the police who are dedicated to fights crime, there are people who are highly experienced. So it is not that we have a shortage of the right people, it is just that we have this leadership crisis. We can’t wait any longer for the Development Plan recommendations in this regard to be implemented. The longer we wait the longer the problems will continue.

Rodney Krotz: Well she had a life cover, which we can’t claim because they need to know what the cause of death was. V/O: Police investigations such as this one, that yield no results are worrying. Even more worrying is the fact that Krotz sister’s case is not isolated – there are countless others. And contributing to this are backlogs in processing evidence, for example there is currently a backlog of 23 000 DNA samples. Gareth Newham of the Institute for Security Studies says the Police’s investigative capabilities have been deteriorating steadily. Gareth Newham: The evidence that there has been a deterioration in the South African Police Service since 2012 is in the annual reports. You see big reductions in the detection rate for example in 2012 the detection rate for murder was almost 32%. Which means that they were able to solve 32% of the cases reported. It has dropped to 20% in the most recent report and you see that for other crimes. V/O: South Africa’s crime investigation and forensic services are suffering in a number of problem areas. CRIME SCENE INVESTIGATION V/O: Crime scene investigators have reported that conditions in the South African Police Service have deteriorated to such an extent that they cannot investigate crime properly. Nationwide CSI officers have basically run out of fingerprint brushes and powders. SOURCE 1: But at the end of the day, we don’t have any powders, we don’t have any brushes, we don’t have any lifters. Due to the procurement process. LINK: This is a complete fingerprint kit. It has all the brushes, the powders, the lifting tape. But these are in short supply in SA because no tender has been awarded to several years. V/O: Brigadier Vish Naidoo is the Police spokesperson. He says it’s a dispute with a supplier that’s resulted in the police service procuring consumables not through tenders, but on an ad hoc basis, through requests for quotations. Vish Naidoo: There has been, not a shortage, but a reduction of consumables, because we can only buy the consumables as and when they are needed. V/O: But the allegations go further. LINK: We were told that special light sources to detect bodily fluids and fingerprints have not been maintained and most are not serviceable because the supplier has not been paid. V/O: Brig Naidoo says when there were allegations of corruption against the supplier, the police terminated the contract. All of this affects the processing of fingerprints nationwide. Gareth Newham: The total number of fingerprints that the police can sue to positively identify suspects in the last three years has declined by 45%. This means that there is almost 15 000 fewer positive hits on fingerprints in cases than there was 3 years ago in 2016/2017. More disturbingly the other forensic exhibits related to DNA, drug testing we’ve seen a massive decline the last three years. 202 000 fewer exhibits were analysed in the most recent financial year, than what was the case three years ago. These are not impressions; these are hard data the police provide and present itself to parliament on its performance. FORENSIC SCIENCE LABS V/O: Allegations have also surfaced around a lack of consumables and lack of maintenance at forensic laboratories that are exacerbating backlogs. Ferdinand Truter, a criminal defence lawyer, has seen backlogs cause delays in court and hamper convictions. Masa: In your experience, would you say there is a backlog in DNA tests blood tests, toxicology? Ferdinand Truter: Definitely, of a normal arrest for intoxication if you get a first appearance today and toxicology reports have been requested, the matter will be postponed between 6 and 12 months. Q: In the forensic Crime lab in Pretoria is the automated DNA system fully functional? Vish Naidoo: The automated, yes the automated DNA system, it’s got various stations. Alright. And I must tell you for each one there are consumables required. So we have to make sure that the consumables are there, which they are. As I said we buy them on procurement, on a quotation basis and the stations are working, the DNA stations. The backlog is not a growing backlog. So as we are moving forward the backlog is getting lesser and lesser. V/O: However, a leaked Information Note signed by three high ranking officials on 13 November, states that the machine is not functional through a lack of specialised consumables, and the absence of a contract for the repair and maintenance of instrumentation. We posed that to Brig Naidoo by e-mail after his interview, but he said he wouldn’t respond to us any further. DIGITAL FORENSICS LICENSES V/O: The field of Digital Forensics has suffered problems for years. Licences for critical software have not been renewed. It was reported in the media last year, but virtually nothing has been done – which seriously hampers digital forensic investigations. SOURCE 2: If you do not have a current license, you do not get updates. You need updates. to access the newer devices and computers with the latest security features. If you are not updated, you cannot extract data from new model cell phones, hard drives or computers. Masa: Can I just ask. In terms of your renewed licences. I want to go through a list of the following products and you tell me if you’ve got renewed licences here. XRY? Vish Naidoo: Um, just hold on there. That information was not requested from me, which I thinks is a bit disingenuous on your part, and therefor I would not be able to tell you which have and which does not have. V/O: But ours was not a disingenuous question – we had requested information around specific licences from Brig Naidoo by e-mail on September 6 and in several other e-mails and text messages. BULLETS V/O: Reports surfaced over the last two years that the police have nearly run out of bullets as their supplier, DENEL, had stopped manufacturing. A shortage means that officers could not qualify to obtain permits to carry weapons, and many had to work without firearms. Vish Naidoo: The problem has since been resolved. We have entered into a 3 year contract with them. We already started to take delivery of ammunition in quite significant amounts. FDA V/O: In 2017 the Police stopped payments to Forensic Data Analysts, the supplier of two important IT systems called the Firearm Permit System or FPS and the Property Control and Exhibit Management system or PCEM. They said it was because of fraud, but no evidence has been produced to substantiate the claim. LINK: The FPS and PCEM systems are absolutely crucial for the functioning of the police and have relevance for the entire criminal justice system. SOURCE 2 FPS is a biometric system that logs in police members, and keeps track of all firearms issued to the police. PCEM keeps electronic track of millions of exhibits and evidence. It secures and track the chain of custody of evidence. V/O: After months of non-payment FDA switched off the systems in April 2018. But the Police and the State Information Agency brought the systems back online. Court cases up to the constitutional court level ordered the Police in scathing terms to either stop using the systems, or pay FDA to acquire the systems. This has not happened. Source 2: It is still being used – illegally. V/O: The two parties are currently in court-ordered talks. FDA declined to comment Q: The court rules that you do owe them money as SAPS. Vish Naidoo: Yes, but we are in discussion with them. We are in discussions with them and I said to you, I am not going to discuss with you or expose what discussions were are in. They know exactly what we are agreeing on. V/O: Shortages of basic crime investigation consumables seem to have been caused by the police avoiding the tender process and procuring goods and services through a quotation-based system. In addition, the Police returned R1,1 billion not spent, to Treasury last year. Can this situation be improved or turned around? One way is to appropriate new technologies to address backlogs and help in the fight against crime. V/O: Jerenique Bayard of Intsika IT says there is amazing new technology available that can rapidly process DNA, yielding results in 90 minutes instead of weeks or months. Jerenique Bayard: When you arrest a person and you can hold him for 48 hours, the DNA act allows you to take a sample from him. But if you then get a result back 6 months later to say that guy is linked to other crimes, to find that guy again is the most difficult task. V/O: Having the results in less than 2 hours, is a real game changer. Jerenique Bayard: The sooner you know this is a person of interest and you can link that person to other cases, the quicker the case will be resolved. V/O: Policing can also benefit from a revision of the top structure of a police service that has grown out of proportion. The National Development Plan addresses this as a priority. Gareth Newham: As far back as 2012 the NDP identifies the serial crisis of the top management in the South African Police Service. For too long people have been appointed in key posts, top posts, without being properly vetted, without being properly assessed. And so now you’ve got this top structure which is quite large, you are talking about 200 generals. And we do not know how many of them should or should not be there. And that is why this issue now with the procurement is one of a whole range of areas where the police have deteriorated. V/O The NDP recommends a Police Board to reassess all those in top positions to make sure the right people are appointed in the right positions. That could turn the police around. Gareth Newham: It is possible to improve the police. There are really good people in the police who are dedicated to fights crime, there are people who are highly experienced. So it is not that we have a shortage of the right people, it is just that we have this leadership crisis. We can’t wait any longer for the Development Plan recommendations in this regard to be implemented. The longer we wait the longer the problems will continue.

metadata.Summary: It seems that even good police officers cannot do their jobs properly because where procurement is supposed to happen, things have grinded to a halt. Most software is not licensed.No new tenders are awarded for crucial consumables, and crucial systems have been ordered to shut down for non-payment. All of it compromises the Criminal Justice system in its entirety
